solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Greek character and relations — about 100 — work together

indicators.note: a thing placed about another goes around it, so the earlier words wrap the next one

blocks.note: mu is a letter of the Greek alphabet
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred
kin are your relatives

explanation.surface: Someone combines a Greek letter with family members and a number, as if describing a fraternity pulling together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' does not mean roughly here: the first two words together go around the number, which lands at their join.
explanation.definitionFit: To muck in is an informal British phrase for joining in and sharing the labour with others.

clue.text: Smart little Maureen, good-looker?

blocks.note: Mo is a short form of the name Maureen
a dish is slang for an attractive person

explanation.surface: Someone admires young Maureen as a well-dressed beauty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smart' looks like a description of Maureen's brains or clothes, but it stands alone as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Modish means fashionable or stylish, which is the clothing sense of smart.

clue.text: Illegally trading criminal gang, one with external difference

definitions.note: the answer is a noun for a smuggler; the definition is the whole phrase describing that person

indicators.note: something external lies on the outside, so this word sits around the others

blocks.note: a contrast is a marked difference
a band is a group or gang
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A gang of criminals trading illegally, one of whom stands out from the rest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Criminal' belongs with the definition, not the wordplay; 'gang' and 'one' sit inside the word for difference, which splits after its sixth letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A contrabandist is a smuggler, someone who deals in goods traded against the law.

clue.text: At home greet fantastic number

indicators.note: something fantastic is wild and unreal, so these letters are rearranged freely

blocks.note: to be in is to be at home
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A host welcomes a great crowd of guests at their house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fantastic number' reads as a huge crowd, but 'fantastic' works on the letters before it and 'number' is the definition alone.
explanation.definitionFit: An integer is a whole number, with no fractional part.

clue.text: French painter of peasants in grass

blocks.note: first meaning: the nineteenth-century realist who painted rural labourers such as The Gleaners
second meaning: a cereal grass grown for its small seeds

explanation.surface: A French artist paints country workers out in the fields.
explanation.walkthrough: The scene of peasants in grass is apt, since Millet painted field workers and his name is also a field crop.
explanation.definitionFit: Millet names both the nineteenth-century French realist artist and a cultivated cereal plant of the grass family.

clue.text: I had left with little sign of hesitation as one with no desire for work

definitions.text: one with no desire for work

blocks.note: I'd is the contraction of 'I had'
L is the standard abbreviation for left
er is the short sound people make when hesitating

explanation.surface: Someone confesses they quit a job after a moment's hesitation, being too lazy to work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I had left' reads as quitting, but it splits into a contraction and a one-letter abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: An idler is a lazy person who avoids effort and prefers doing nothing.

clue.text: Careless kids — acacia all messed up

indicators.note: a thing messed up is jumbled out of order, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Thoughtless children have trampled and wrecked an acacia tree.
explanation.walkthrough: All thirteen letters of the three words after the dash are used.
explanation.definitionFit: Lackadaisical describes someone lacking enthusiasm and effort, which shades into being careless or negligent.

clue.text: Maybe watch circling bird initially in wood

indicators.note: to circle something is to go right round it, so one part encloses another
initially means at the start, so only the opening letter is kept

blocks.note: a watch can serve as a timer, hence 'maybe'
the first letter of bird

explanation.surface: A birdwatcher in a forest watches a bird wheeling overhead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maybe' flags a definition by example: a watch is one kind of timer.
explanation.definitionFit: Timber is wood prepared or grown for building and carpentry.

clue.text: Meant not to be caught in act

indicators.note: a thing caught in something is held inside it

blocks.note: taken as written
a deed is an act

explanation.surface: Someone insists they never intended to be caught in the act.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Caught in the act' is a stock phrase, but here 'act' must become a synonym that holds the word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: To denote is to signify or indicate, so denoted is a past-tense synonym of meant.

clue.text: Went down river, having gone outside

indicators.note: to be outside something is to surround it, so one word goes around the other

blocks.note: R is the standard abbreviation for river
gone is a euphemism for dead

explanation.surface: A boat travelled downstream after having gone outside first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Went down river' reads as one phrase about a journey, but the definition stops at 'down'.
explanation.definitionFit: Decreased means became smaller or lower, a past-tense synonym of went down.

clue.text: See copper, male officer standing in?

blocks.note: lo is an old word meaning look or see
Cu is the chemical symbol for copper
M is the standard abbreviation for male

explanation.surface: Look at the policeman, a man covering someone else's shift.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' wants to be a police officer, but it is the metal; the question mark admits the officer is loosely a professional.
explanation.definitionFit: A locum is a doctor or cleric who temporarily fills in for a colleague who is absent.

clue.text: Child in frivolous programme

indicators.note: the letters wanted sit inside the following words, running across them

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: A child appears in a silly television show.
explanation.walkthrough: A sprog is a British slang word for a child.
explanation.definitionFit: Sprog is informal British slang for a young child or baby.

clue.text: My sons get old bouquet

blocks.note: cor is a British exclamation of surprise, like 'my!'
S is the abbreviation for son, here standing for the plural too
to age is to grow old

explanation.surface: A parent laments that their sons are getting older.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My' looks possessive but is the exclamation 'My!', and the British equivalent is cor.
explanation.definitionFit: A corsage is a small bunch of flowers worn pinned to clothing or on the wrist.

clue.text: City pub cold with no ale unfortunately

indicators.note: an unfortunate outcome is things going wrong, so the letters fall into a different order

blocks.note: a bar is a pub
C is the abbreviation for cold, as on taps
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A drinker grumbles that the city pub is chilly and has run out of beer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No ale' reads as a complaint, but those five letters are the material that 'unfortunately' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: Barcelona is a major Spanish city, the capital of Catalonia, so it is an example of the category.

clue.text: Old boy with lines in face (moneyed type)

blocks.note: OB is the abbreviation for old boy, a former pupil
lines of poetry make up verse

explanation.surface: A rich old gent has a wrinkled face.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lines in face' suggests wrinkles, but 'in' is only a link and the face is the kind on money, as the bracket hints.
explanation.definitionFit: The obverse is the side of a coin bearing the head or principal design, its front face.

clue.text: Short brat struggling to keep up

indicators.note: something struggling twists and writhes, so its letters are thrown into a new order
to keep something is to hold it, so one part is held inside another

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
taken as written

explanation.surface: A small, unruly child finds it hard to keep pace with everyone else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short brat' reads as a small child, but 'Short' is the definition, in the sense of curt.
explanation.definitionFit: Abrupt means brief and curt in manner, the same as short when someone is being rude.

clue.text: No gentleman quietly set up in place of confinement

indicators.note: in a down clue, setting something up raises it so it reads from bottom to top

blocks.note: taken as written
sir is the title for a gentleman
p is piano, the musical direction to play quietly

explanation.surface: A cad is quietly framed and ends up locked away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set up' suggests framing someone for a crime, which suits the jail, but here it turns the letters upward.
explanation.definitionFit: A prison is a building where convicted people are held, so it is a place for confinement.

clue.text: Fruit and nuts

blocks.note: first meaning: the long yellow tropical fruits
second meaning: slang for crazy

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fruit and nuts' reads like a snack mix; 'nuts' is the slang adjective for mad, not a food.
explanation.definitionFit: Bananas is a plural fruit, and also informal slang for insane or wildly excited.

clue.text: French city enthrals English relative

indicators.note: to enthral is to captivate, holding someone in its grip

blocks.note: Nice is a city on the French Riviera
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: A French city charms a visiting English family member.
explanation.walkthrough: The city name is spelt like the English adjective nice, which may hide it.
explanation.definitionFit: A niece is a daughter of one's brother or sister, a family member.

clue.text: Facial guard — it is taken from guest

indicators.note: something taken from a whole is removed, leaving the remainder

blocks.note: a visitor is a guest
taken as written; these letters are removed

explanation.surface: A protective mask, it turns out, was taken from a houseguest.
explanation.walkthrough: The word 'it' is itself the letters lifted out of the middle of VISITOR.
explanation.definitionFit: A visor is the movable front of a helmet or a shield that protects the face.

clue.text: Weld in section of gun I tested

indicators.note: a section is a part of a longer string, so the letters lie within the words

blocks.note: the letters run across all three words

explanation.surface: A welder joins part of a firearm that someone has just test-fired.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Weld' is a verb here, matching the verb hidden in the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: To weld is to join pieces firmly together, so it is a synonym of combine.

clue.text: Terrible performances with no leader or rules

indicators.note: a leader comes first, so without one the opening letter is dropped

blocks.note: dire means terrible
acts are performances; lose the first letter

explanation.surface: A critic slams dreadful shows that lack a star or any rules.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No leader or rules' reads as anarchy, but the deletion ends at 'leader' and 'rules' is the verb definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To direct and to rule both mean to govern or control, as in issuing orders.

clue.text: Tear sleeve of T-shirt off for rag

indicators.note: a sleeve covers the outside, so only the outer letters are kept
off means wrong or not right, so the letters go out of order

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
the first and last letters of T-shirt

explanation.surface: Rip the sleeve off a T-shirt to make a cleaning cloth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tear' looks like an instruction to rip, but it is anagram fodder; 'sleeve' is the outer edge of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: A tatter is a torn scrap of cloth hanging loose, which is what a rag is.

clue.text: Magician’s bird of prey

blocks.note: first meaning: the wizard of the King Arthur legends
second meaning: a small falcon

explanation.surface: A wizard keeps a pet hawk.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s looks possessive, but it stands for 'is', linking the two meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: Merlin is the legendary Arthurian wizard and also the name of a small falcon species.
